Hi Lisa —

Thanks, attached is our completed questionnaire and a network topology PDF that highlights the isolation boundaries. Below is a concise summary (we put the long-form answers in the attached PDF):

1) Isolation model (high level)
- Hardware Partitioning Groups (HPGs): customers can be pinned to dedicated GPU HPGs when required (Dedicated offering) to provide physical device-level segmentation.
- Logical tenancy: in multi-tenant Hosted mode we use namespace-level isolation (K8s namespaces + CNI network policies) plus process-level sandboxing. Each tenant is assigned a unique tenant ID namespace enforced end-to-end.
- Control plane separation: customer control plane operators are logical constructs that do not have access to inference host file systems; customer metadata is stored in a separate, access-restricted store.

2) Network topology & egress controls
- Private link + customer-side VPC peering: we support AWS PrivateLink and comparable constructs to avoid public internet traversal for API traffic.
- Egress staging: outbound model artifact downloads and package fetches occur from a restricted build-host pool through an egress gateway with allowlisting and deep packet inspection (DPI) rules.
- Egress policies per-tenant: Envoy-based sidecars enforce token-scoped egress allow/deny lists and block all outbound DNS by default unless explicitly allowed.
- Customer-managed NAT and fixed egress IPs: for customers requiring fixed outbound IPs we provide an egress proxy cluster with published IPs or support placement into customer-managed subnets.

3) KV cache and data handling
- Per-tenant KV namespaces with AES-256-GCM at rest. Keys are wrapped with a root key in a cloud KMS; we support customer-managed KMS keys (CMKs) and HSM-backed wrapping on Private deployments.
- In-flight encryption: all inter-service traffic uses mTLS with mutual authentication and per-call auth tokens. We also sign cache entries and validate TTLs to prevent replay/poisoning attacks.

4) Threat model summary (top risks -> controls)
- Risk: Lateral movement from compromised admin host.
  Control: Role-based admin separation, jump-host bastions with ephemeral credentials, OS-level attestation for hosts, and aggressive segmentation of management plane traffic.
- Risk: KV cache poisoning during active batches.
  Control: Signed cache entries, sequence number checks, and strict validation at cache read; anomalous hit-rate alerts trigger immediate cache eviction and traffic reroute.
- Risk: Data exfil via model outputs.
  Control: Output redaction policies, model-level output filters, and per-tenant usage anomaly detectors; customers can enable output sinks that require approval.

5) Auditability & evidence
- We provide immutable request logs (with redaction controls), token-level cost traces, and optional extended retention for compliance. For Private deployments we can ship full audit bundles.

Lisa — quick answers below, and we can expand in the walkthrough.

1) HPG availability
- HPGs are only provisionable as part of our Dedicated offering. Host-level hardware partitioning with pinned GPUs requires reservation of Dedicated capacity. In Hosted we provide strong logical isolation (namespace + sandboxing) and may offer pinned instance pools as a paid add-on in specific regions — we noted a roadmap item for physical tenancy-on-demand but it is not generally available today.

2) CMK rotation for KV namespaces
- When a customer uses a CMK, keys used to wrap per-tenant KEKs are rotated on a scheduled cadence (configurable; default 90 days). Rotation is performed by the cloud KMS; during rotation we perform seamless rewrap operations with no downtime to KV operations. We log each rotation event and provide signed rotation attestations. For Private deployments customers may elect to trigger rotation windows themselves.

3) Log redaction and reconstruction risk
- Example: request metadata logs include request_id, tenant_id (hashed at rest), model_id and top-level timing metrics. Full request payloads are not logged by default; if a customer requests payload logging it is stored in an encrypted vault with access controls and requires RBAC approval.
- We do not store raw token streams in standard logs; any derived tokens are salted and hashed using tenant-scoped salts. To be clear: standard logs are designed to prevent reassembly; we classify payload logging as a high-risk feature requiring explicit customer opt-in and an approval workflow.

Next: I'll drop a calendar invite for Thu 8/9 10:00 PT and include a short 10-slide deck that walks through the HPG lifecycle and our egress proxy controls. If you need the audit snippets faster, Sean can send a redacted sample log bundle.
